name: Norse
line: Meet your fate with courage, keep your word and open your door.

quote.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one’s self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
quote.source: The Poetic Edda, Hávamál, stanza 77, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

quotes.text: A better burden may no man bear for wanderings wide than wisdom; it is better than wealth on unknown ways, and in grief a refuge it gives.
quotes.source: The Poetic Edda, Hávamál, stanza 10, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

quotes.text: If a friend thou hast whom thou fully wilt trust, and good from him wouldst get, thy thoughts with his mingle, and gifts shalt thou make, and fare to find him oft.
quotes.source: The Poetic Edda, Hávamál, stanza 44, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

quotes.text: The witless man is awake all night, thinking of many things; care-worn he is when the morning comes, and his woe is just as it was.
quotes.source: The Poetic Edda, Hávamál, stanza 23, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

quotes.text: The lame rides a horse, the handless is herdsman, the deaf in battle is bold; the blind man is better than one that is burned, no good can come of a corpse.
quotes.source: The Poetic Edda, Hávamál, stanza 71, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

quotes.text: The sun turns black, earth sinks in the sea, the hot stars down from heaven are whirled.
quotes.source: The Poetic Edda, Völuspá, stanza 57, trans. Henry Adams Bellows, 1923

words.meaning: Fate; what has come to be
words.usage: Also the name of one of the three Norns who tend the well under the world tree.

words.meaning: The first-laid law; one’s allotted fate
words.usage: What was set down at the beginning. Even the gods live under it.

words.meaning: Luck, as a force that runs in a person or a family
words.usage: Luck could be lent, inherited and worn out. In modern Icelandic the word means happiness.

words.meaning: Honour; the bearing of a good man or woman
words.usage: Fairness, courage and generosity together. The highest praise in the sagas is to be called a good drengr.

words.meaning: Peace, above all the peace among kin
words.usage: More than the absence of fighting: the bond that makes a household safe.

words.meaning: Mind, heart and courage in one
words.usage: The seat of thought and of nerve. To have a good hugr is to be both kind and brave.

words.meaning: A poet
words.usage: Skalds served kings, and a good verse could save a life. Egill composed one overnight to keep his head.

words.meaning: A poetic name made of two words
words.usage: The sea is the whale-road, a ship is a wave-horse, gold is Sif’s hair.

words.meaning: A tale; literally, what is said
words.usage: The long prose stories written in Iceland in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

words.meaning: The name of two books of myth and poetry
words.usage: The Poetic Edda is a collection of old poems. The Prose Edda is Snorri’s handbook for poets. The meaning of the word is disputed.

words.meaning: An assembly of free people
words.usage: Where law was recited, cases were heard and deals were struck. The word survives in the names of Nordic parliaments.

words.meaning: The general assembly of Iceland
words.usage: Founded about 930 at Þingvellir. Iceland’s parliament still carries the name.

words.meaning: A chieftain who also led worship
words.usage: In Iceland the office could be bought, shared and inherited, and followers were free to change chieftain.

words.meaning: An offering feast
words.usage: A sacrifice followed by a shared meal. Modern Heathens use the word for a rite of offering.

words.meaning: A formal round of drinking and toasts
words.usage: A horn goes round. Each person speaks over it: to the gods, to the dead, to a promise.

words.meaning: A kind of magic concerned with fate and foresight
words.usage: Practised mostly by women, and by Odin. What it involved is known only in outline.

words.meaning: A seeress
words.usage: A travelling woman with a staff who was asked to see what was coming. The poem Völuspá is spoken by one.

words.meaning: A secret; a letter of the runic alphabet
words.usage: The same word means mystery and written sign.

words.meaning: The world tree
words.usage: An ash that holds all the worlds, watered by the Norns and gnawed at root and branch.

words.meaning: The middle enclosure: the world of people
words.usage: Fenced off from the wild outside and ringed by a serpent in the sea.

words.meaning: The enclosure of the gods
words.usage: Home of the Æsir, joined to the human world by the bridge Bifröst.

words.meaning: The fate of the gods
words.usage: The last battle, in which the gods fall and the earth sinks, and after which a green world rises.

words.meaning: The hall of the slain
words.usage: Odin’s hall, where chosen warriors feast and train for the last battle. Most of the dead went elsewhere.

words.meaning: One of the women who shape fate
words.usage: Three sit at the well, named for what was, what is becoming and what shall be.

words.meaning: A follower: a spirit that goes with a person
words.usage: Often seen as an animal or a woman, and sometimes in dreams before a death.

words.meaning: The spirits of the land
words.usage: Icelandic law once told ships to take down their dragon heads so as not to frighten them. Four of them stand on Iceland’s coat of arms.

words.meaning: Yule: the midwinter feast
words.usage: Days of drinking and oath-taking at the darkest time of the year. The Nordic word for Christmas still comes from it.

words.meaning: Mead
words.usage: Honey, water and time. In the myths, the mead of poetry makes anyone who drinks it a poet.

words.meaning: A bowl; a toast
words.usage: Still the Scandinavian word when glasses are raised.

words.meaning: The game of the king’s table
words.usage: A board game in which a king at the centre tries to break out through a ring of attackers.

words.meaning: A broad cargo ship
words.usage: The ship that carried settlers, livestock and timber across the North Atlantic.

words.meaning: A sea expedition for trade or plunder
words.usage: Something a person went on. Most people of the age were farmers who never did.

practices.name: Morning counsel
practices.instructions: Before the day starts, read one stanza of the Hávamál, the sayings of the High One. Read it twice, the second time aloud. Put it in your own words in a single sentence, and decide where in today it might apply: a meeting, a meal, a quarrel. Take the stanzas in order from the first, one each morning. They begin with a guest arriving at a door.
practices.why: The Hávamál is the closest thing the Norse world left to a book of advice. It is practical and dry: how to be a guest, how much to drink, whom to trust. One verse a morning is how such counsel was meant to be carried.
variations: Write the stanza on a card and keep it in your pocket.
Learn one stanza by heart each week.
Read the Old Norse aloud alongside the translation, for the sound.

practices.name: Out in all weather
practices.instructions: Go outside for twenty minutes whatever the sky is doing. Dress for it properly and leave the headphones behind. Walk until you are warm. Notice the wind direction, the light and one thing that has changed since yesterday. If it is foul, go anyway and come back to something hot. The only rule is that the weather does not get a vote.
practices.why: People of the North lived by reading sea, sky and season, and the old poems are full of weather. Going out daily without waiting for a good day builds the plain hardiness the sagas admire.
variations: Walk to water: a shore, a river, a canal.
Go at first light or last light.
Take someone with you and say little.

practices.name: Handwork
practices.instructions: Spend twenty minutes making or mending something with your hands. Whittle a spoon, sew on a button, sharpen the kitchen knives, knit a row, oil a hinge, patch a jacket. Choose one piece of work and keep to it across the days so you can watch it grow. Work without a screen. Stop when the time is up, and leave the tools ready for tomorrow.
practices.why: A Norse household made nearly everything it used, and skill of hand was honoured in farmers and in kings alike. A well-made, well-kept thing was a form of reputation.
variations: Carve your initial in runes on something you made.
Learn one sound knot and use it.

practices.name: Open door
practices.instructions: Do one act of hospitality each day. Offer a drink and a seat to whoever comes to your door. Share your food with a colleague. Ask a new neighbour in. Give a traveller directions and walk them to the corner. On a day when no one comes, send word to someone who is alone. The Hávamál lists what a guest needs: fire, food, dry clothes, water, a towel and a welcome.
practices.why: In a land of long roads and hard winters, turning a traveller away could kill them. Hospitality was law and honour together, and the Hávamál opens with it.
variations: Keep something in the house to offer at short notice.
Invite one person to eat with you this week.
Be a good guest in return: arrive on time, leave in good time.

practices.name: Evening telling
practices.instructions: At the end of the day, tell it as a saga would. Three or four sentences, in the past tense, with no adjectives you do not need and no account of feelings: only who did what and what was said. Say it aloud to someone, or write it down. Then read or listen to ten minutes of a real saga or a poem from the Edda, and let that be the last thing in your head.
practices.why: The sagas tell terrible and funny things in the same level voice and leave the judging to the listener. Telling your own day that way takes the self-pity out of it and shows what actually happened.
variations: Give the day a title, as saga chapters have.
Tell it to a child as a story.
Compose one kenning for something you saw today.

tasks.name: Write your name in runes
tasks.meta: Elder Futhark, on paper or scrap wood

tasks.name: Sharpen a blade or mend something you own
tasks.meta: A knife, an axe, a boot, a seam

tasks.name: Learn to tie a bowline and use it once
tasks.meta: The knot that does not slip

tasks.name: Read the first twenty stanzas of the Hávamál aloud
tasks.meta: Read · the guest at the door

tasks.name: Listen to Helvegen with your eyes shut
Journal: what will be said of you when you are gone?
If the ending were already fixed, what would you still do today?
Splash your face with cold water outdoors
Raise a glass to someone absent and say their name
Whittle, carve or peel something with a knife, carefully
Tell a tall tale about your day at dinner
Look at the wind and the sky and decide what kind of day it is
Say the name of someone you honour

rules.text: Give every guest a seat, a drink and a welcome
rules.why: The first stanzas of the Hávamál are about the stranger at the door. Whoever comes in today, see to them before yourself.
The wise guest in the poem keeps quiet, listens and looks. Speak when you have something to add, and let one silence stand today.

rules.text: Give your word rarely and keep it wholly
rules.why: An oath was sworn on a ring and remembered for generations. Promise one thing fewer today, and do every one you promise.
The Hávamál says the more a man drinks, the less he knows his own mind. Stop one before you would have.

rules.text: Answer a gift with a gift
rules.why: Friendship in the poems is kept alive by exchange. If someone gave you time, food or help, give something back within the day.
The poem says to praise a day when it is over, ice when it is crossed and ale when it is drunk. Finish the work before you talk about it.

read.title: The Poetic Edda
read.creator: trans. Carolyne Larrington
read.year: poems written down about 1270; this translation 2014
read.why: The old poems themselves: the seeress’s vision of the beginning and end, Odin’s sayings, Thor in a wedding dress. Start with Völuspá and Hávamál.

read.title: The Prose Edda
read.creator: Snorri Sturluson, trans. Jesse Byock
read.why: An Icelandic chieftain’s handbook for poets, and the source of most of the myths as they are told today.

read.title: Njal’s Saga
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Robert Cook
read.why: The greatest of the sagas of Icelanders: a fifty-year feud that law, friendship and good sense all fail to stop.

read.title: Egil’s Saga
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Bernard Scudder
read.why: The life of a warrior-poet who was ugly, greedy, violent and the finest skald of his age.

read.title: The Saga of the Volsungs
read.creator: Anonymous, trans. Jesse Byock
read.why: Sigurd, the dragon and the cursed gold. The tale behind Wagner’s Ring and much of Tolkien.

read.title: Children of Ash and Elm
read.creator: Neil Price
read.why: A history of the Viking Age by an archaeologist, told from the inside: what they believed, feared and wore.

read.title: Norse Mythology
read.creator: Neil Gaiman
read.why: The myths retold plainly and well, close to the sources. A good first book.

watch.title: The Northman
watch.creator: Robert Eggers
watch.why: A revenge saga filmed with archaeologists at the director’s elbow. The clothes, halls and rites are as near as film has come.

watch.title: When the Raven Flies
watch.creator: Hrafn Gunnlaugsson
watch.why: An Icelandic film in the bleak, dry manner of the sagas, shot on the black sands where they are set.

watch.title: Vikings Unearthed
watch.creator: NOVA, PBS
watch.why: A documentary on how far west the Norse sailed, and on the search for a second site in North America.

watch.title: Valhalla Rising
watch.creator: Nicolas Winding Refn
watch.why: A near-wordless film of a mute warrior carried over the sea. Harsh and strange, and not for every evening.

listen.title: Runaljod – Yggdrasil
listen.creator: Wardruna
listen.why: Music built on old Nordic instruments: bone flutes, goat horn, lyre and frame drum. The album includes Helvegen, a song for the road of the dead.

listen.title: Edda: Myths from Medieval Iceland
listen.creator: Sequentia
listen.why: An attempt to sing the Eddic poems as they may once have sounded, in Old Norse, with harp and fiddle.

listen.title: Rímur
listen.creator: Steindór Andersen
listen.why: Icelandic chanted verse, a tradition unbroken since the Middle Ages, sung by its best-known modern voice.

listen.title: Der Ring des Nibelungen
listen.creator: Richard Wagner
listen.why: Fifteen hours of opera drawn from the Volsung saga and the Eddas. A nineteenth-century German dream of the North, and the origin of the horned helmet.

art.title: The Oseberg ship
art.creator: Buried in 834, Norway
art.why: An oak ship with a spiral prow, buried with two women, a cart, sledges and tapestries. It is held by the Museum of the Viking Age in Oslo.

art.title: The Lewis chessmen
art.creator: Walrus ivory, probably carved in Norway
art.why: Wide-eyed kings, queens and shield-biting warriors found on a Hebridean beach. Shown in the British Museum and the National Museum of Scotland.

art.title: The Jelling stones
art.creator: Jelling, Denmark
art.why: Two rune stones raised by King Gorm and his son Harald Bluetooth, the second with the oldest image of Christ in Scandinavia.

art.title: Gotland picture stones
art.creator: Gotland, Sweden
art.why: Tall carved slabs showing ships under sail, riders welcomed with a horn and scenes from lost stories.

art.title: Urnes stave church portal
art.creator: Luster, Norway
art.why: A doorway of interlaced beasts biting each other, carved for an earlier church and kept. It gave its name to the last Viking art style.

eat.title: Skyr
eat.creator: Thick cultured milk, with berries
eat.why: Made in Iceland since the settlement and mentioned in the sagas. Eat it with bilberries or a spoon of honey.

eat.title: Flatbread
eat.creator: Rye or barley, baked on a hot pan
eat.why: The daily bread of the North. Mix flour, water and salt, roll it thin and cook it dry.

eat.title: Barley porridge
eat.creator: With butter
eat.why: The plain staple of farm and ship. Simmer it slowly and stir in butter at the end.

eat.title: Dried or smoked fish
eat.creator: With butter or on rye bread
eat.why: Wind-dried fish kept through winter and was traded across Europe. Smoked mackerel or herring is the nearest thing in most shops.

eat.title: Lamb and root vegetable soup
eat.creator: A long-simmered pot
eat.why: Lamb, turnip, onion and herbs, in the spirit of the cauldron that hung over every hearth.

drink.title: Mead
drink.creator: Honey wine, or honey in warm water
drink.why: The drink of halls and poems. A spoon of honey in hot water with a slice of apple is the version without alcohol.

drink.title: Buttermilk or whey
drink.creator: Cold
drink.why: The everyday drink on a dairy farm. Sour whey was also used to preserve food.

drink.title: Small ale
drink.creator: Or a malt drink without alcohol
drink.why: Weak ale was drunk daily by everyone. Any dark malt drink stands in well.

customs.title: The round of toasts
customs.creator: A horn or cup passed hand to hand
customs.why: At a feast each person speaks over the drink in turn: thanks, remembrance of the dead, a promise. Try one round at your own table, with any drink.

customs.title: Gift for gift
customs.creator: Exchange that keeps a friendship
customs.why: A gift called for a gift in return, of fitting size. Too large a gift could shame the receiver.

customs.title: The guest’s three nights
customs.creator: A welcome with a limit
customs.why: A traveller was owed shelter, and good manners kept the stay short. The Hávamál warns that the loved guest becomes loathed if he sits too long.

customs.title: Naming what you rely on
customs.creator: Ships, swords and halls had names
customs.why: Things that carried a life were given names and treated with care. Name a tool, a bicycle or a boat.

games.title: Hnefatafl
games.creator: Board game · Norse
games.why: A king and his guard at the centre, twice as many attackers at the edges. The king wins by reaching a corner. Rules are reconstructed, and boards are easy to draw.

games.title: God of War
games.creator: Video game · Santa Monica Studio
games.why: A father and son walk through the nine worlds to scatter a mother’s ashes. The myths are bent freely and treated with unexpected tenderness.

games.title: Assassin’s Creed Valhalla: Discovery Tour
games.creator: Video game · Ubisoft Montreal
games.why: A combat-free tour of Viking Age Norway and England, with quests on farming, trade, law and belief written with historians.

games.title: Valheim
games.creator: Video game · Iron Gate
games.why: Build a hall, sail a longship into fog and live through the weather. It captures the pleasure of timber, fire and a safe roof.

festivals.title: Þorrablót
festivals.creator: Late January to late February, Iceland
festivals.why: A midwinter feast revived in the nineteenth century, with the old preserved foods, verses and song.

festivals.title: Up Helly Aa
festivals.creator: Last Tuesday of January, Lerwick, Shetland
festivals.why: A torchlit procession of a thousand guizers that ends with the burning of a galley. The form is Victorian, the islands’ Norse past is real.

festivals.title: Midsummer
festivals.creator: Around 21 to 24 June, across Scandinavia
festivals.why: Bonfires, flowers and a night that barely darkens. The feast is far older than any name it has carried.

festivals.title: Jorvik Viking Festival
festivals.creator: February, York, England
festivals.why: A week of living history, craft and talks in the city that was the Norse capital of northern England.

places.title: Þingvellir
places.creator: Iceland
places.why: The rift valley where the Icelanders met each summer from about 930 to make law in the open air. A World Heritage Site.

places.title: Viking Ship Museum
places.creator: Roskilde, Denmark
places.why: Five original ships raised from the fjord, and a boatyard that builds and sails full-size reconstructions.

places.title: Jelling
places.creator: Jutland, Denmark
places.why: Two royal mounds, the rune stones and a church between them. The place where Denmark names itself for the first time.

places.title: Birka
places.creator: Björkö, Lake Mälaren, Sweden
places.why: A trading town of the eighth to tenth centuries reached by boat from Stockholm, with thousands of grave mounds.

places.title: L’Anse aux Meadows
places.creator: Newfoundland, Canada
places.why: The one confirmed Norse site in North America. Tree rings show wood was being cut there in the year 1021.

places.title: Lofotr Viking Museum
places.creator: Borg, Lofoten, Norway
places.why: A chieftain’s longhouse 83 metres long, rebuilt on the spot where it was found.

ethics.title: The open door
ethics.text: A traveller is owed fire, food and a welcome. The Hávamál begins here, and it treats the way you receive a stranger as the measure of your house.
ethics.practice: Offer food or drink to the next person who comes through your door, before they ask.

ethics.title: A name that outlives you
ethics.text: Possessions and people pass. What remains is what is said of how you acted. Norse ethics is less about rules than about being someone of whom a good story can be told.
ethics.practice: Before a decision today, ask how it would sound told plainly to your grandchildren.

ethics.title: The kept word
ethics.text: Oaths bound families for generations, and oath-breakers have the worst place in the afterlife the seeress describes. A promise is a debt.
ethics.practice: List every promise you have outstanding. Keep one today or release it honestly.

ethics.title: Gift and return
ethics.text: Friendship is made of exchange: visits, help, gifts, time. The poem says to go often to a friend’s house, because weeds grow on the path no one walks.
ethics.practice: Visit, call or write to a friend whose path has grown over.

ethics.title: Measure
ethics.text: The Hávamál praises the middle: enough food, enough drink, enough wisdom. It warns that the over-wise are seldom glad.
ethics.practice: Stop one thing today while it is still good: a meal, a drink, an argument.

ethics.title: Courage without hope of reward
ethics.text: The gods know they will lose the last battle and prepare for it anyway. Doing right is not made pointless by a bad outcome.
ethics.practice: Do one right thing today that you expect to get no credit for.

philosophy.title: Fate and the free hand
philosophy.text: What will happen is laid down, and the Norns have cut it. What is left to you is how you meet it, and that is where all honour lies. The sagas admire people who walk into a known end with a joke.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing you cannot change this week. Write one sentence on how you intend to meet it.

philosophy.title: The world ends, and the work goes on
philosophy.text: Norse myth is unusual in telling of the gods’ defeat. Odin gathers warriors knowing it will not be enough. The meaning lies in the stand and not in the result.
philosophy.practice: Do today’s work as if it mattered whether or not it lasts.

philosophy.title: Wisdom is paid for
philosophy.text: Odin gave an eye for a drink from the well of wisdom and hung nine nights on the tree to win the runes. Nothing worth knowing came free, even to a god.
philosophy.practice: Choose one thing you want to understand. Decide what you will give up this week to make room for it.

philosophy.title: Middling wise
philosophy.text: Three stanzas of the Hávamál say a person should be wise in measure, never too wise. Whoever sees their fate too clearly has no easy heart.
philosophy.practice: Leave one question unresearched today. Notice whether you are lighter for it.

philosophy.title: The gnawed tree
philosophy.text: The world tree holds everything and is eaten at every moment: a serpent at the root, deer in the branches, rot in the trunk. The world is sustained and wearing out at once, and it is tended anyway.
philosophy.practice: Tend one thing today that is slowly wearing out: a friendship, a tool, your own back.

philosophy.title: Luck is a thing you build
philosophy.text: Hamingja was luck, and also something like stored worth. It grew with good dealing, could be lent to a friend on a journey and passed to a child with a name.
philosophy.practice: Do one thing today that adds to the luck of someone younger than you.

philosophy.title: With law the land is built
philosophy.text: A saying found in Njal’s Saga and in old Nordic law: with law shall the land be built up, and with lawlessness laid waste. Free people settled disputes by argument at the assembly, when it worked.
philosophy.practice: Settle one disagreement today by terms both sides can state aloud.

journal: Who came to your door today, in any sense, and how did you receive them?
What would be said of today if it were told in three plain sentences?
Which promise are you carrying, and how does it stand?
What did you make or mend with your hands?
Where did you say more than you knew?
What can you not change, and how did you meet it?
Who gave you something today, and what will you give back?
What was the weather, and what did it ask of you?
When did you stop at enough, and when did you not?
Whose path to your house has grown over with grass?
What did you do today that took some nerve?
Which stanza stayed with you, and where did it apply?
What are you paying for the thing you most want to know?
What name would you give to a tool or thing you rely on?
Who are your kin, by blood or by choice, and what do you owe them?
What would you do differently if no one would ever hear of it?
What is wearing out around you that deserves tending?
When were you a good guest today?
What did you listen to in silence?
What quarrel could be settled by stating terms aloud?
What did the dark part of the day give you?
Which of your possessions would you want buried with you, and why?
What piece of luck did you inherit, and from whom?
Where did you wait to praise until the thing was done?
What story do you tell about yourself that a saga would cut?
What do you want to be known for in your own street?
What did you learn from an older person this week?
Which fear turned out smaller when you walked up to it?
What would you carry on a long crossing, and what would you leave?
What will you still do, knowing how it ends?
reflect: What did living by an open door change in your house?
Which rule was hardest to keep, and what did that show you?
What did you make or mend in these days, and what will you keep making?
How has your view of fate, luck and effort shifted?
What do you now want to be said of you?
Which stanza or story will you carry forward?

intro: The Norse were the people of Scandinavia in the centuries before and during its conversion to Christianity. They were farmers and fishers first. Some were also traders, settlers, poets and raiders, and in the age we call Viking they reached Baghdad by river and North America by sea. This Onda is about how they saw the world: a view built on fate, reputation, hospitality and a dry, unsentimental courage.

They had no single holy book and no word for religion. They spoke of custom. There were many gods, among them Odin, who sought wisdom at any price; Thor, who defended the human world; and Freyja and Freyr, who gave love and harvest. There were also spirits of land and family, honoured at the farm. Worship meant offerings and shared feasts, led by the head of the household or a chieftain, outdoors or in the hall.

Nearly everything we can read about this world was written down later, by Christians, mostly in Iceland. Around 1220 the chieftain Snorri Sturluson wrote a handbook for poets that retells the myths. Around 1270 someone copied a collection of old poems into the small manuscript now called the Codex Regius. The sagas, long prose stories about the settlers of Iceland and their feuds, were written in the same century. These sources are precious and are not neutral. Archaeology fills in the rest: ships, graves, rune stones, combs and gaming pieces.

What comes through is a moral world without a promise of rescue. The gods themselves will die at Ragnarök, and they know it. Fate is fixed and cannot be bargained with. What is left to a person is conduct: to keep faith with kin and friends, to be generous to a guest, to speak little and carefully, to hold to a promise and to face what comes without complaint. A good name is the one thing that outlasts death.

The practices here are taken from that everyday ethic, above all from the Hávamál, the poem of advice put in Odin’s mouth. You will read a stanza each morning, go out in all weather, work with your hands, keep an open door and tell your day plainly at night. Nothing here is a religious rite. Heathenry is a living religion today, in Iceland and elsewhere, and its rites belong to its communities.

One more thing needs saying. In the last two centuries Norse symbols have been taken up by nationalist and racist movements, from the Nazis to groups active now. That use is a modern invention. The Viking world was a trading world that married, borrowed and settled across every border it crossed.
guide.origin: Scandinavia, and the places its people settled: Iceland, the Faroes, Greenland, the British Isles and the rivers of the east
guide.era: The Viking Age, about 750 to 1100, with roots centuries older and written sources from thirteenth-century Iceland

figures.name: Snorri Sturluson
figures.bio: Icelandic chieftain, lawspeaker and writer. His Prose Edda preserved the myths and his Heimskringla the lives of the Norwegian kings. He was killed in his own cellar on the orders of one of them.

figures.name: Egill Skallagrímsson
figures.bio: Farmer, fighter and the greatest skald of the Viking Age. His lament for his drowned son, Sonatorrek, is one of the first personal poems in a northern language.

figures.name: Aud the Deep-Minded
figures.bio: A queen’s widow who had a ship built in secret, sailed her household from Scotland to Iceland and took a whole district, giving land and freedom to those who came with her.

figures.name: Thorgeir Thorkelsson
figures.bio: Lawspeaker of Iceland and a pagan priest. Asked to rule between the old faith and the new around the year 1000, he lay under a cloak for a day and a night and chose one law for all, to keep the peace.

figures.name: Gudrid Thorbjarnardóttir
figures.bio: Called the far-traveller. She sailed to Greenland and to Vinland, where her son was born, and in old age walked to Rome.

figures.name: Leif Eriksson
figures.bio: Son of Erik the Red. Around the year 1000 he led the first known European landing in North America.

figures.name: Harald Bluetooth
figures.bio: King who united Denmark and, as his rune stone at Jelling says, made the Danes Christian. A wireless standard carries his name.

figures.name: Saxo Grammaticus
figures.bio: Danish cleric whose Latin history of the Danes gives other versions of the myths, and the first telling of the story of Hamlet.

figures.name: Brynjólfur Sveinsson
figures.bio: Bishop of Skálholt who came into possession of the Codex Regius in 1643 and saw what it was. Without him the Eddic poems might be lost.

figures.name: Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson
figures.bio: Icelandic farmer and poet, master of the old chanted verse. In 1972 he founded Ásatrúarfélagið, which won recognition for the old religion in Iceland the following year.

history.detail: A comb found in a Danish bog at Vimose carries one of the oldest runic inscriptions known: a single name. Runes stayed in use for well over a thousand years.
Seaborne raiders attacked a monastery off the coast of Northumbria. Writers at the time treated it as a shock, and later historians made it the opening date of the Viking Age.
Two women were buried in southern Norway in a richly carved ship with animals, wagons and textiles. It is the finest grave of the age, and no one knows who they were.
Families from Norway and the British Isles began to settle an empty island. Within sixty years the usable land was taken.
The Icelanders set up a general assembly at Þingvellir, with a lawspeaker who recited the law from memory. There was no king.
Harald Bluetooth raised a great carved stone saying he had won all Denmark and made the Danes Christian. Conversion in the North was slow and came mostly from the top.
Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland, led settlers to the fjords of south-west Greenland. The colony lasted more than four hundred years.
With the country close to splitting, the Althing accepted Christianity by the decision of a pagan lawspeaker. Private worship of the old gods was allowed for a time.
Tree rings from L’Anse aux Meadows show that Norse people were felling trees there in exactly this year, the earliest precise date for Europeans in the Americas.
Harald Hardrada of Norway died invading England. The date is the conventional end of the Viking Age.
Two centuries after the conversion, an Icelandic chieftain set down the old myths so that young poets could still understand the old images.
An unknown scribe copied twenty-nine poems about gods and heroes into a small plain book. It is the main source of the Poetic Edda.
Denmark returned the Codex Regius and Flateyjarbók to Iceland by warship. Crowds lined the harbour in Reykjavík and the day was shown live on television.
Iceland gave official standing to Ásatrúarfélagið, founded the year before. It is now one of the largest religious groups in the country outside the national church.

concepts.text: The ash tree that holds the worlds.
concepts.detail: Its three roots reach to three wells. An eagle sits at the top, a serpent gnaws below and a squirrel carries insults between them. The Norns water it daily. The image is of a universe that is alive, suffering and cared for.

concepts.text: Three women who shape what will be.
concepts.detail: Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld sit at the well and cut the fate of every child. Nothing in the myths can overrule them, not Odin and not prayer. The ethical weight therefore falls on how a fate is met.

After three winters with no summer, the bound wolf breaks loose, the serpent leaves the sea and the gods fight a battle they lose. The earth sinks. Then it rises again green, and two people who hid in the tree begin once more.

The Æsir, among them Odin, Thor and Frigg, are tied to rule, war and wisdom. The Vanir, among them Njörðr, Freyr and Freyja, are tied to sea, harvest and desire. The myths say they fought, made peace and exchanged hostages.

Warriors chosen by Odin feast in Valhalla, and Freyja takes half the slain to her own field. Most people went to Hel, a quiet realm under the earth with a ruler of the same name. It was not a place of punishment.
The opening of the Hávamál sets out what a traveller needs and how host and guest should behave. Odin himself was said to walk the roads in disguise, which gave every stranger a certain weight.

In a society without police or prisons, standing was a person’s protection. An insult had to be answered, a debt paid and a promise kept, or the family’s worth fell. The sagas show the cost of this as clearly as its dignity.

Free farmers met at local and national assemblies to hear the law, bring cases and arrange settlements. There was no force to carry out a verdict, so enforcement fell to the winning side, and feuds grew from that gap.

concepts.text: Poetry as a craft of riddles.
concepts.detail: Court poets worked in tight metres with internal rhyme and layered names. To follow a verse you needed the myths, which is why Snorri wrote them down.

concepts.text: Letters cut in wood and stone.
concepts.detail: The older alphabet had twenty-four signs and the Viking Age one sixteen. Most inscriptions are memorials, ownership marks and messages: this stone was raised for a good brother; Gyda says you should go home.

facts.text: No horned helmet has ever been found in a Viking grave. The horns were added by a costume designer for the first complete staging of Wagner’s Ring in 1876.
Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are named in English after Tyr, Odin, Thor and Frigg, in their Old English forms.
The Bluetooth symbol joins two runes, the initials of King Harald Bluetooth, who joined Denmark and Norway.
Combs, tweezers and ear spoons are among the most common finds in Norse graves. The Old Norse word for Saturday, laugardagr, means washing day.
A piece of wood from Bergen, carved about 1200, reads: Gyda says you should go home. It was probably sent to a husband in the tavern.
Iceland’s parliament, the Althing, traces its founding to about 930, which makes it one of the oldest in the world.
The poem Völuspá says that after the end of the world the gods will find their golden gaming pieces lying in the grass.

sensitivity.note: The old Norse religion is known mainly through texts written by Christians two centuries after the conversion, and it is also a living religion today, known as Heathenry or Ásatrú. This Onda draws on the everyday ethics of the sources. It does not offer religious rites, and it rejects the use of Norse symbols by racist movements.
requiredCaveats: The sources are late and partial. Much of what is said about Norse belief is reconstruction, and scholars disagree.
Heathenry is practised today. Its rites belong to its communities; nothing here imitates them.
Runes and other Norse symbols have been used by Nazi and white-supremacist groups. That use is modern and has nothing to do with the Viking Age.
The Viking Age included raiding, killing and a large trade in enslaved people. The sagas’ ideals of honour sat alongside that.
This content has not yet been reviewed by scholars of Old Norse or by Heathen communities. It should be before release.
